content: Malnutrition is a frequent complication in children and adolescents with cancer, often resulting from the malignancy itself or as a side effect of chemotherapy. Nutritional support is designed to address malnutrition present at diagnosis, prevent treatment-related malnutrition, and support weight gain and growth. However, the most effective and safest methods of nutritional support in this population remain unclear. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of parenteral nutrition (PN) and enteral nutrition (EN), excluding vitamin and micronutrient supplementation, in children and adolescents with cancer undergoing chemotherapy. Additionally, the review aimed to assess the impact of the nutritional content of PN and EN. This is an updated version of a previous Cochrane review. The search for relevant studies included multiple databases, such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others, covering the period from 2006 to September 2013. Experts in the field were also consulted, and reference lists of included articles were reviewed to identify additional trials. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing different forms of nutritional support or comparing nutritional support to a control group in children and adolescents with cancer undergoing chemotherapy. A total of 14 trials were included in the review, involving 595 participants under the age of 21 with leukemia or solid tumors undergoing chemotherapy. Most of the trials were of low quality, except for two studies on glutamine supplementation. One small trial demonstrated that PN, compared to EN, significantly increased weight (mean difference [MD] 4.12 kg, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.91 to 6.33), serum albumin levels (MD 0.70 g/dL, 95% CI 0.14 to 1.26), calorie intake (MD 22.00 kcal/kg/day, 95% CI 5.12 to 38.88), and protein intake (MD 0.80 g/kg/day, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.15). Another trial comparing peripheral PN and EN with central PN found that the peripheral PN and EN group had significantly lower mean daily weight gain (MD -27.00 g/day, 95% CI -43.32 to -10.68) and energy intake (MD -15.00 kcal/kg/day, 95% CI -26.81 to -3.19), but a significantly greater increase in serum albumin levels (MD 0.47 g/dL, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.81, P = 0.008). A small trial found that children receiving an energy-dense feed had a higher mean energy intake (28% above the recommended daily amount, 95% CI 17% to 39%) compared to those receiving a standard-calorie feed. However, the evidence for glutamine supplementation was inconclusive. Two studies showed no statistically significant reduction in the severity of mucositis (relative risk [RR] 0.64, 95% CI 0.19 to 2.2; and RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.1), and two studies found no significant differences in infection rates (RR 1.0, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.4; and RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.51). One study compared olive oil-based PN to standard lipid-containing PN. Despite similar calorie contents, the standard lipid formula resulted in greater weight gain (MD -0.34 z-scores, 95% CI -0.68 to 0.00). Another study compared standard EN with fructooligosaccharide-containing EN and found no difference in weight gain between the groups (MD -0.12, 95% CI -0.57 to 0.33). Adverse effects, such as nausea, occurred at similar rates in both groups (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.74). In conclusion, there is limited evidence to suggest that PN is more effective than EN in well-nourished children and adolescents with cancer undergoing chemotherapy. Evidence supporting other methods of nutritional support remains unclear. Limited data suggest that energy-dense feeds may increase daily energy intake and promote weight gain. The evidence for glutamine supplementation in reducing mucositis, infection rates, or hospital stay is not statistically significant. Further research with larger sample sizes and rigorous methodologies is urgently needed to provide more definitive guidance.
